summary: Describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange protocol, a component of IPsec used to authenticate both sides and to set up and maintain security associations. It replaced RFC 4306 and folded in the clarifications from RFC 4718. It was itself replaced by RFC 7296.

plainLanguage.summary: IKEv2 lets two IPsec peers authenticate each other and agree on keys and algorithms. They use that initial agreement to establish and maintain security associations for protected traffic.

questions: how does ipsec key exchange work
subtitle: How IPsec peers authenticate and establish security associations.

tldr.problem: IPsec peers need shared keys, algorithms and other state before they can protect IP traffic; configuring all of this manually does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: IKEv2 authenticates two peers and establishes an IKE security association. It then creates, rekeys and deletes Child SAs for ESP or AH traffic.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5996 replaced RFC 4306 and RFC 4718 with clarifications and small protocol changes. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7296.

today: RFC 5996, a Proposed Standard, has been obsoleted by RFC 7296. It was updated by RFC 5998 and RFC 6989, and obsoleted RFC 4306 and RFC 4718.

sections.title: What IKEv2 Establishes
sections.content:
IPsec protects IP datagrams by using shared state that identifies the services, algorithms and keys for traffic. Internet Key Exchange (IKE) establishes this state dynamically instead of requiring manual setup.

IKE authenticates both peers and creates an IKE security association (SA). It can then establish Child SAs for Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) or Authentication Header (AH), and can negotiate IP compression.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec needs peers to agree on how to protect traffic and which keys to use. IKEv2 performs that agreement and authenticates both peers.

sections.title: The Initial Exchanges
sections.content:
Communication normally starts with two request/response exchanges: IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH. IKE_SA_INIT negotiates algorithms, exchanges nonces and performs a Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

IKE_AUTH exchanges peer identities and authentication data, then establishes the first Child SA. The IKE_AUTH payloads are encrypted and integrity-protected using keys derived from the initial exchange. The usual start therefore contains four messages.
sections.plainLanguage: First, the peers agree on algorithms and exchange information used to derive keys. Then they authenticate their identities and set up the first protected traffic association.

sections.title: Messages and Payloads
sections.content:
IKE messages contain a fixed header followed by payloads. The header includes initiator and responder SPIs, version, exchange type, flags, a Message ID and total message length. Message IDs match requests with responses and identify retransmissions.

IKE uses UDP port 500 and can also use port 4500 for NAT traversal. IKE messages are request/response pairs; the requester retransmits if it does not receive a response in time.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies the security association, exchange and message number. IKE peers use message numbers to match replies and recognize retransmissions.

sections.title: Creating, Rekeying and Deleting SAs
sections.content:
After setup, CREATE_CHILD_SA can create a Child SA or replace an existing IKE or Child SA. Rekeying creates a new association before deleting the old one, and can include another Diffie-Hellman exchange.

INFORMATIONAL exchanges carry notifications, delete SAs or perform housekeeping. A request with no payloads can check whether the other peer is still responding. Deleting an IKE SA also closes its remaining Child SAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers can create new protected traffic associations after the initial setup. They can replace old associations, report information or delete associations through later exchanges.

sections.title: Protection and Denial-of-Service Controls
sections.content:
IKE messages use UDP, so the protocol includes handling for packet loss, replay and forged packets. When a responder sees many half-open IKE SAs, it should send a cookie and require the initiator to retry with it.

The cookie exchange lets a responder check that the initiator can receive traffic at its claimed address before keeping state for the negotiation. The RFC also requires implementations to process messages up to 1280 octets and recommends support up to 3000 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: A responder can ask an initiator to return a cookie before continuing a connection setup. This helps limit the work caused by forged requests.
